corrected_value.authors: Linkenauger S. A., Witt J. K., & Proffitt D. R.
corrected_value.title: Taking a hands-on approach: Apparent grasping ability scales the perception of object size.

decisions.location: Abstract, Line 1; Introduction, Line 2; General Discussion, Line 2; References, Line 10
decisions.quote: Linkenauger, Witt, and Proffitt (2011) found that the perceived size of graspable objects was scaled by perceived grasping capacity. However, it is possible that this effect occurred because object size was estimated on the same trial as grasping capacity. This may have led to a conflation of estimates of perceived action capacity and spatial properties. In 5 experiments, we tested Linkenauger et al.’s claim that right-handed observers overestimate the grasping capacity of their right hand relative to their left hand, and that this, in turn, leads them to underestimate the size of objects to-be-grasped in their right hand relative to their left hand.
decisions.reason: Collier and Lawson (2017) empirically retest two distinct original articles by Linkenauger and colleagues: (1) Linkenauger, Witt, Bakdash, Stefanucci, and Proffitt (2009, Psychological Science, DOI 10.1111/j.1467-9280.2009.02447.x, 'Asymmetrical Body Perception'), which is represented in shipped_rows row 1931 and coded as target_index 0 (retested in Experiment 1 on perceived hand-size asymmetry and in the perceived grasping capacity tasks); and (2) Linkenauger, Witt, and Proffitt (2011, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 37, 1432-1441, DOI 10.1037/a0024248, 'Taking a hands-on approach: Apparent grasping ability scales the perception of object size.'), which is coded as target_index 1 and is the central study retested across Experiments 2-5 investigating whether right-handed observers' greater perceived grasping capacity for the right hand scales visually perceived object size of graspable blocks ('Thus we did not replicate the results of Linkenauger et al. (2011) because we failed to find the predicted influence of perceived action capacity on spatial perception'). Luna triage erred by conflating target_index 1 (Linkenauger et al., 2011) with shipped row 1931 (Linkenauger et al., 2009). Linkenauger et al. (2011) is a separate published study and is genuinely missing from shipped_rows. Prior adjudication and state files do not exist for this work.
